newsitem.title: FINLAND: Belgium, Finland try to meet French EMU concerns.
newsitem.headline: Belgium, Finland try to meet French EMU concerns.

text.p: Belgium and Finland joined Germany on Wednesday in signalling readiness to do more than listen sympathetically to France's view that job creation should carry more weight in the European Union's economic and monetary union (EMU).

Prime ministers Jean-Luc Dehaene of Belgium and Paavo Lipponen of Finldand said they were prepared to support an addition to the Maastricht treaty's article 103, which envisages coordination of EU member countries' economic policies.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said earlier Bonn was not opposed to adding a jobs chapter to the Maastricht treaty.

"When you have a specification about how the (EMU convergence) criteria have to go further after the start of monetary union, it is also logical to say how the coordination of economic policies will be organised," Dehaene told a news conference.
He was referring to the EMU budget stability pact designed to enforce fiscal discipline once a single currency is launched in 1999.
Dehaene was visiting Finland as part of a tour of EU capitals ahead of the June 16-17 summit of heads of state and government in Amsterdam.

France's new socialist government has said it needs more time to review the stability pact, raising doubts whether EU leaders will be able to approve wide-ranging reforms in a revised treaty designed to prepare the bloc for its ambitious expansion eastward.

Lipponen said Belgium and Finland had tried "to reach consensus on the issues which France has brought up" and they agreed that employment and the social dimension should have more prominent status in the stability pact.

"We are prepared to discuss some extension or protocol in the spirit of article 103...so that we could have a more coordinated policy," Lipponen said. "It would oblige member countries to streamline their policies to do more for employment."
Kinkel had said: "Of course we are not opposed to a jobs chapter. It is obvious that everything possible must be done to counteract the intolerably high level of unemployment."
Germany had previously opposed the idea of a jobs chapter, fearing political interference in the work of a future independent European central bank.

Lipponen described the German policy shift as "very positive" and said that agreement on a text giving more operational effect to article 103 also meant "that we support the independence of the (European) central bank."

Dehaene said any new protocol should be agreed speedily. "I don't think there is a big difficulty," he said. "The only problem is to have that(new text) concrete and have it concrete on time so that you do not create a period of uncertainty."
Dehaene and Lipponen both said they did not want to touch the stability pact as such and they backed the German view that it could not be renegotiated.
